opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to know yourself, and that's harder than it sounds, because we all have two yous. There's the you that's the logical, conscious you, and then there's the emotional you, the one that's kind of below the surface and wired in a certain way. A lot of people go through life never really having that honest conversation with themselves, so they pursue what they think they're supposed to want.

So I'd start by asking: what is your nature? We're all born differently. Some people are big-picture thinkers and some are very detail oriented. Some are creative, and some are terrific at reliably following through. None of that is good or bad. It's like nature gave us different tools, and an elephant shouldn't try to be a cheetah. There are personality assessments that can help you, and I'd take them, but I'd also ask the people who know you well, "What do you see as my strengths and my weaknesses?" Then really listen, even when it's hard to hear.

The second thing is to experiment. You won't figure this out by sitting and thinking about it. You try things, you make mistakes, and you pay attention to what happens. I think of life as a kind of loop: you go after something, you fail, you reflect on that pain, you learn, and you come back better. Pain plus reflection equals progress. And notice what pulls you. When you're doing the thing that fits your nature, you don't need someone pushing you. The work itself has a pull, and you want to keep getting better at it. For me, that was markets. I started when I was twelve, caddying at a golf course and hearing people talk about stocks, and it was like a game I just loved playing.

Then there's a question I think people should ask early, which is, "What's the life I actually want?" Life comes in phases. In the first, you're dependent on others and you're learning. In the second, you're working and others are depending on you. In the third, you're free. A young person is at the very start of that arc, so don't confuse the job with the goal. Think of work as a means to the life you want, and choose your path with that in mind.

And lastly, get around people who are strong where you're weak, and who will be honest with you. Because you don't have to be good at everything. You just have to know what you don't know, and find the people who do. That was probably the most important thing I ever learned.

r001.rationale: The response says to choose work with the life you want in mind, but it does not mention financial considerations or say they must remain part of the choice.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a person’s nature with what they think they are supposed to want, then describes nature through characteristic ways of thinking, such as being big-picture or detail-oriented.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you have to know yourself, and most people don't. I think the biggest mistake young people make is they think about what they should do before they think about who they are. They look at what pays well, or what their parents want, or what looks impressive, and they try to fit themselves into that. And it doesn't work, because nature is stronger than will.

So I'd start with this. Pay attention to what you're drawn to and what you're good at, and notice that those are two different things. What you're drawn to tells you what your motivation will be. What you're good at tells you what your capabilities are. Where those overlap, that's where you want to be looking. If you love something but you're mediocre at it, you'll struggle. If you're great at something but you hate it, you'll burn out.

The second thing is, you have to get in the game. You can't figure out your nature by sitting in a room thinking about it. You have to go out and do things, and then you fail, and then you learn. I had a saying at Bridgewater, pain plus reflection equals progress. When something goes badly, that's when the information shows up. Most people run from the pain. They don't want to look at it. But if you can train yourself to say, okay, what does this tell me about me, about how I'm wired, about what I need to change or what I need to work around, that's the whole game. Your mistakes are your best teachers because they're the most honest.

And the third thing, which took me a long time to learn, is that you need people around you who are strong where you're weak. I'm a certain kind of person. I'm a big picture, visualize-it-and-go-after-it kind of person. I'm not great at the details. For a while I thought I had to be good at everything, and that was a mistake. Once I understood my nature, I could build around it. I could find people who were different from me and value them instead of fighting them.

So if I had to put it simply, it's this. Be radically honest with yourself about what you are. Go make mistakes, and reflect on them rather than hiding from them. And then don't try to be someone else. The world is full of people trying to be someone else, and it's a miserable way to live. Find out what you are and then become the best version of that.

r001.rationale: The response calls choosing what pays well a mistake and does not say financial considerations should remain part of a passion aligned career choice.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes motivation from capability and gives an example of a big picture thinking style, but does not clearly distinguish a person's nature from their preferences.

astra-6.text:
I think you start by getting to know yourself through experience. What are you naturally curious about? What kinds of problems do you enjoy working on, even when they’re difficult? And where do you struggle, despite putting in a lot of effort?

When you’re young, you don’t have enough information to answer all of that. So try things. Work with different people. Pay attention to your reactions, and ask people who know you well for honest feedback. Sometimes they can see your strengths and weaknesses more clearly than you can.

Then distinguish what you actually want from what other people have taught you to want. It’s very easy to pursue a career because it brings approval or status, and discover that you don’t enjoy the life that comes with it.

You’re looking for a fit between your nature, work you find meaningful, and people you enjoy working with. You won’t get it exactly right at first. Make a choice, learn from what happens, and adjust. That process of discovery is part of finding your path.

r001.rationale: The response discusses approval, status, and career fit, but does not say financial considerations should remain part of the choice.

r002.rationale: It asks about curiosity, enjoyable problems, and learned wants, but does not distinguish nature from preferences by describing nature as characteristic ways of thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with being curious about yourself. What are you drawn to? What do you enjoy doing enough that you’ll keep doing it when it gets difficult? And what are you actually good at? Those aren’t necessarily the same things.

When you’re young, you don’t have to settle that immediately. Try things. Have experiences. Pay attention to what gives you energy, and ask people who know you well for honest feedback. Sometimes other people can see your strengths and weaknesses more clearly than you can.

Then you’re looking for a fit between your nature and what you do. You can get better at things, of course, but you don’t want your whole life to be a struggle against who you are. And discovering that fit is a process. You make a choice, you learn something about yourself, and you adjust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interests, abilities, and career fit but does not mention financial considerations.

r002.rationale: The response refers to a person's nature without describing it as characteristic ways of thinking or distinguishing it from preferences.
